units.title: Beginnings
units.subtitle: Ancestors, Canaan and the two kingdoms

lessons.title: The ancestors
lessons.check_note: Bereshit Rabbah 38:13 read on Sefaria 11/14. Seder Olam date for Abraham, the camel finding and the scholarly dating are from memory: check.

cards.title: A family story in one sentence
cards.body: When an Israelite farmer brought the first fruits to the sanctuary, they told the whole family history in a single line, beginning with a wanderer.

cards.q: What does the Bible say Abraham's father Terah did?
choices: Served as a priest of the one God
cards.why: Joshua says the ancestors "lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods."

cards.gloss: "My father was a fugitive Aramean" (26:5). The Passover Haggadah builds its telling of the Exodus on these three words.

cards.title: The idol shop
cards.body: The midrash fills in Joshua's hint. **Terah sold idols.** One day he left young Abraham to mind the shop. A customer came in; Abraham asked his age. Sixty, said the man. Abraham answered: a man of sixty, bowing down to something made **yesterday**? The man left, ashamed. The story ends with Abraham smashing the idols.

cards.q: In Bereshit Rabbah 38:13, why is the idol buyer ashamed?
choices: Abraham shows him he is older than the god he is buying
cards.why: A grown man bowing to a thing **a day old**: Abraham's first argument is a question.

cards.body: Seder Olam, a 2nd-century chronology, puts Abraham's birth in year **1948** from Creation.

src.note: 1656 years to the Flood (read on Sefaria) + 292 to Abraham; check.

cards.body: Most scholars date the **writing** of the ancestor stories to these centuries, from older oral traditions.

src.ref: e.g., Finkelstein & Silberman, The Bible Unearthed (2001)

cards.title: What historians can say
cards.body: No inscription or dig has found **Abraham, Sarah, Isaac or Jacob**. Some details fit an early age (names, travel from Mesopotamia to Canaan). Others fit a later one: **domesticated camels** in Canaan date to about 1000 BCE, centuries after the traditional date. Many scholars read Genesis as a people's **memory of its origins**, written down long after.

src.ref: Camel bones: Sapir-Hen & Ben-Yosef, Tel Aviv 40 (2013)

cards.q: What have archaeologists found about Abraham?
choices: No inscription or find that names him
A letter he wrote in Ur
cards.why: The ancestors are known **only from the Bible** and later tradition.
wrong_why: The tomb at Hebron is a tradition, not an inscription.

src.ref: Camel bones: Sapir-Hen & Ben-Yosef, Tel Aviv 40 (2013)

cards.title: Two questions
cards.body: **Did it happen?** and **What does it mean?** are different questions. History works on the first; the tradition answers the second through the story. This track keeps both, side by side, and labels each card: Tradition, Scholars, Reform.

src.ref: Reform approach to text and history

cards.body: In every Amidah you name the ancestors: Elohei Avraham, Elohei Sarah. The Genesis lessons tell their stories.

cards.prompt: Your family has its own one-sentence story of where you came from. What is it, and which part do you know is true?

points: "**My father was a fugitive Aramean**" (Deut 26:5).
Joshua 24:2: the ancestors **worshiped other gods**.
Midrash: Abraham in **Terah's idol shop**.
No inscription names the ancestors; scholars date the **writing** much later.

lessons.title: Israel in Canaan
lessons.check_note: Jerusalem Talmud Sheviit 6:1 and Bava Batra 14b read on Sefaria 11/14. Merneptah Stele date, village survey and Deuteronomistic History are from memory: check.

cards.title: After Moses
cards.body: The book of **Joshua** tells of a fast conquest. The book of **Judges** tells of a slow, messy settling in, tribe by tribe, with many Canaanites still in the land.

cards.q: Where does the name Israel first appear outside the Bible?

cards.title: Three letters
cards.body: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman: before crossing the Jordan, **Joshua sent three messages**. Whoever wants to leave, leave. Whoever wants to make peace, make peace. Whoever wants to fight, fight. The Girgashites left, and went to Africa.

cards.q: In the Jerusalem Talmud, what three choices did Joshua offer the peoples of Canaan?
cards.why: The rabbis gave Joshua's wars **a way out**.

cards.gloss: "In those days there was no king in Israel" (21:25). Judges ends with this line, and it points ahead to the kings.

cards.body: Pharaoh **Merneptah** boasts that Israel is wiped out: the first mention of Israel outside the Bible.
Hundreds of **small new villages** appear in the hill country of Canaan: the age of the Judges.

cards.title: The stone and the villages
cards.body: On the stele, Israel is written with the sign for **a people**, not a city: a group, already in Canaan. The new hill villages share simple **four-room houses**, and their bones show **no pigs**. Many scholars think most early Israelites grew up **inside Canaan**; others argue a smaller group did come out of Egypt, carrying the Exodus story with them.

src.ref: e.g., Dever, Who Were the Early Israelites? (2003)

cards.q: On the Merneptah Stele, Israel is marked as a people rather than a city. What does that suggest?
choices: Israel was a group living in Canaan, not yet a city-state
Israel was a kingdom with a capital
cards.why: A people **in the land** by about 1208 BCE.
wrong_why: The stele places Israel in Canaan.

src.ref: e.g., Dever, Who Were the Early Israelites? (2003)

cards.title: Who wrote these books?
cards.body: **Tradition**: Joshua wrote his own book and the last eight verses of the Torah; Samuel wrote Judges and Ruth (Bava Batra 14b). **Scholars**: Joshua through Kings form one long history, edited around the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, judging each age by Deuteronomy's laws.

src.ref: Bava Batra 14b; scholars: Noth, the Deuteronomistic History (1943), check

cards.gloss: "I and my household will serve GOD" (24:15). Joshua's last speech asks the people to **choose this day**.

cards.body: Deborah judged Israel in these years. Her story is in the Torah stories track.

cards.prompt: Joshua asks a people to choose, again, what they will serve. What would you say you choose, this year?

points: Joshua: fast conquest; Judges: **slow settling**.
Talmud: Joshua's **three letters**: leave, make peace, or fight.
**Merneptah Stele**, about 1208 BCE: Israel, a people in Canaan.
"**There was no king in Israel**" (Judges 21:25).

lessons.title: The two kingdoms
lessons.check_note: Sanhedrin 102a read on Sefaria 11/14. Tel Dan and Mesha stelae details and dates are from memory: check.

cards.title: Lighten our load
cards.body: After Solomon dies, the northern tribes ask his son **Rehoboam** to lighten the heavy work his father put on them. He answers that he will make it heavier.

cards.q: What did Jeroboam, the first king of the north, set up in Bethel and Dan?
cards.why: "So the king took counsel and made two golden calves" (1 Kings 12:28).

cards.body: **David** rules from Jerusalem; then Solomon builds the Temple.
The kingdom splits: **Israel** in the north, **Judah** in the south, with Jerusalem.

cards.gloss: "To your tents, O Israel!" The north walks away from David's house.

cards.title: Why the calves?
cards.body: Jeroboam's fear was simple: if his people kept going up to **Jerusalem** to worship, their hearts would go back to Judah's king. So he built **his own shrines** at the edges of his land. The book of Kings blames every later northern king for this.

cards.title: God grabs his garment
cards.body: Rabbi Abba: God took hold of Jeroboam by his garment and said, **Repent**, and you and I and the son of Yishai will walk together in the Garden of Eden. Jeroboam asked, "Who will walk in the lead?" "The son of Yishai will walk in the lead." Jeroboam: "If so, I do not wish to repent."

cards.q: In Sanhedrin 102a, why does Jeroboam refuse to repent?
choices: David would walk ahead of him
He did not believe in the Garden of Eden
cards.why: Pride: he would rather **lose Eden than walk second**.

cards.title: The House of David in stone
cards.body: In **1993**, at Tel Dan in the far north, archaeologists found part of a 9th-century BCE stone. In Aramaic, a king of Aram boasts of killing the king of Israel and a king of the **House of David**: the first mention of David outside the Bible. Another stone, the **Mesha Stele**, names Israel's king Omri. How large David's kingdom was is still argued.

src.ref: Tel Dan Stele (Israel Museum); Mesha Stele (Louvre)

cards.q: What does the Tel Dan Stele show?
choices: David's dynasty was known outside the Bible
cards.why: "**House of David**" in a 9th-century enemy's inscription.
wrong_why: No plan of the Temple has been found.

src.ref: Tel Dan Stele (Israel Museum); Mesha Stele (Louvre)

cards.body: Elijah's stories happen in the northern kingdom, under Omri's son Ahab. David's own stories are in their unit.

cards.prompt: Rehoboam could have lightened the load and kept the kingdom whole. When has a small act of listening, or not listening, changed things for you?

points: Rehoboam's answer, and "**To your tents, O Israel!**"
Two kingdoms: **Israel** (north) and **Judah** (south), about 930 BCE.
Jeroboam's **golden calves** at Bethel and Dan.
Sanhedrin 102a: "**Who will walk in the lead?**"
Tel Dan: the **House of David** in stone.

units.title: Exile and return
units.subtitle: Assyria, Babylon and the Second Temple

lessons.title: Assyria and the lost tribes
lessons.check_note: Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:3 read on Sefaria 11/14. Sargon's deportation number, Sennacherib's prism, Jerusalem's growth and the Sambatyon sources are from memory: check.

cards.title: Samaria falls
cards.body: Assyria, the great power of its day, besieges **Samaria**, capital of the northern kingdom, for three years.

cards.q: According to Rabbi Akiva in the Mishnah, will the ten lost tribes return?
choices: They already came back with Ezra
cards.why: Rabbi Akiva says no; Rabbi Eliezer disagrees.

cards.body: Assyria conquers **Samaria**. The northern kingdom ends.
Assyria's king **Sennacherib** besieges Jerusalem. The city survives; Judah goes on.

cards.title: What Assyria did
cards.body: Assyria moved conquered peoples around to break them. Its king **Sargon II** claims he carried off about **27,000** people from Samaria, and the Bible says Assyria settled other peoples in their place. Many northerners also **fled south**: Jerusalem grew several times over in these years.

src.ref: Sargon II's annals; Jerusalem's growth: e.g., Broshi (1974)

cards.q: What did Assyria do with the people of Samaria?
choices: Deported many and settled other peoples in their place
wrong_why: The Bible and Assyria's records say otherwise.
They went east, to Assyria and Media.

src.ref: Sargon II's annals; Jerusalem's growth: e.g., Broshi (1974)

cards.title: Will they come back?
cards.body: The Mishnah records a debate. **Rabbi Akiva**: the ten tribes will not return, as it says, "As it is this day": as a day passes and never comes back. **Rabbi Eliezer** reads the same words the other way: as a day grows dark and then **brightens again**, so it will be for them.

cards.q: How does Rabbi Eliezer read "as it is this day"?
choices: A day darkens and then brightens: they will return
A day passes forever: they are gone
They will return on one special day
cards.why: Same verse, **two readings**: an ending, or a night before morning.

cards.title: The search
cards.body: The lost tribes became legend: beyond the river **Sambatyon**, which rests on Shabbat, they live on. Travelers like **Eldad HaDani** (9th century) claimed to come from them. Communities from Ethiopia to India have been linked to a lost tribe.
Each morning in Ahavah Rabbah you pray to be brought "from the four corners of the earth," Isaiah's words. And Jonah's Nineveh was Assyria's great city.

cards.prompt: Rabbi Akiva saw an ending; Rabbi Eliezer saw a night before morning. Which way do you tend to read your own losses?

points: **722 BCE**: Assyria ends the northern kingdom.
Exile and **resettlement**; many flee south to Judah.
Rabbi Akiva: gone like a day; Rabbi Eliezer: **morning comes**.
Isaiah: gathered "**from the four corners of the earth**."

lessons.title: By the rivers of Babylon
lessons.check_note: Mishnah Taanit 4:6, Yoma 9b and Pesachim 87b read on Sefaria 11/14. Dates, the Al-Yahudu tablets and the scholarly view of exile and Torah are from memory: check. Does CBB read Lamentations on Tisha B'Av?

cards.title: The city burns
cards.body: Babylon's king **Nebuchadnezzar** takes Jerusalem, burns the Temple, and carries Judah's leaders away.

cards.q: What did the prophet Jeremiah tell the exiles in Babylon to do?
choices: Build houses, plant gardens, and pray for the city
Fast until the Temple was rebuilt
cards.why: "Build houses and live in them, plant gardens and eat their fruit" (Jer 29:5).

cards.body: First exile: King **Jehoiachin** and Jerusalem's elite are taken to Babylon.
Jerusalem falls. The **First Temple** is destroyed.

cards.gloss: "Alas! Lonely sits the city" (Lam 1:1). The book of Lamentations, read on **Tisha B'Av**, opens with this word, Eichah.

cards.title: Why was it destroyed?
cards.body: The Mishnah lists five disasters on the **Ninth of Av**, among them both Temples destroyed. The Talmud asks why. The First: idolatry, sexual sins and bloodshed. The Second, in an age of Torah and kindness? "**Wanton hatred**," which the Talmud weighs as equal to all three.

cards.q: In Yoma 9b, why was the Second Temple destroyed?
cards.why: Not ritual failure but **how people treated each other**.
wrong_why: The Talmud gives that for the First Temple.

cards.gloss: "Seek the welfare of the city" (29:7). From here come Jewish prayers for the country where Jews live.

cards.q: What does Jeremiah tell the exiles to seek?
choices: The welfare of the city they were exiled to
cards.why: Live **fully** where you are, and pray for it.
wrong_why: Psalm 137 has anger; Jeremiah does not counsel it.
He says the exile will be long.

cards.title: Exile as seed
cards.body: Rabbi Elazar: God exiled Israel among the nations "**only so that converts would join them**": as a farmer sows a little grain to harvest much more.

cards.title: A people without a Temple
cards.body: Clay tablets from Babylonia (the **Al-Yahudu** tablets) record Judean families farming in a village called **Judah-town**, giving their children Hebrew names. Many scholars think that in exile, without Temple or king, Judeans gathered around **texts and prayer**, and much of the Torah took its final shape.
When the Torah returns to the ark, you sing Hashiveinu, from the last chapter of Lamentations: bring us back to You.

cards.prompt: Jeremiah says: build, plant, pray for the place you are, even if it is not home. Where in your life are you being asked to do that?

points: **586 BCE**: the First Temple falls.
Lamentations and Psalm 137: "**If I forget you, O Jerusalem**."
Yoma 9b: the Second Temple fell for **wanton hatred**.
Jeremiah: "**seek the welfare of the city**."
In exile, a people of **text and prayer**.

lessons.title: Return and the Second Temple
lessons.check_note: Bava Kamma 82a (incl. the wilderness origin of Monday/Thursday reading) and Sanhedrin 21b read on Sefaria 11/14. Cyrus Cylinder, 515 BCE and Ezra's dates are from memory: check.

cards.title: A new empire
cards.body: In **539 BCE**, Persia's king **Cyrus** takes Babylon. Soon after, he lets the Judeans go home.

cards.q: According to the Talmud, what changed about the Torah scroll in Ezra's time?
choices: Its script, to the square letters
cards.why: Sanhedrin 21b: the Torah was given again in **Ashurit script**, the square letters you learned.

cards.body: **Cyrus** conquers Babylon and lets exiles return.
The **Second Temple** is finished in Jerusalem.
**Ezra** the scribe and **Nehemiah** the governor rebuild community and walls.

cards.title: Cyrus in his own words
cards.body: Cyrus left his own clay **cylinder**: he says he returned peoples and their gods to their homes. It never names Judeans, but it fits Ezra's story. And many Judeans **stayed** in Babylon, which later became the great center of the Talmud.

cards.q: Did all the exiles go back to Judah?
choices: No, they all went to Egypt
wrong_why: Many stayed; Babylon's community lasted for centuries.

cards.title: Ezra's ordinances
cards.body: The Talmud lists ten rules Ezra made. Among them: read the Torah on **Shabbat afternoon**. The Monday and Thursday readings were older, from the wilderness, so Israel would not go "three days without hearing the Torah." Ezra set the form still used: **three people** read, at least **ten verses**.

cards.q: What does the Talmud say Ezra added to Torah reading?
choices: A reading on Shabbat afternoon, with three readers
The first Monday and Thursday readings
cards.why: Ezra **added and shaped**; the weekday readings were older.
wrong_why: The Talmud says those go back to the wilderness.

cards.title: New letters
cards.body: Mar Zutra: the Torah was first given in **Ivrit** script (the old Hebrew letters). In Ezra's days it was given again in "**Ashurit script**," the square letters still used today. Rabbi Yosei: Ezra was worthy that the Torah could have been given through him, had Moses not come first.

cards.q: Why does the Talmud link Ezra to the square Hebrew letters?
choices: The Torah was given again in Ashurit script in his days
cards.why: The letters you are learning carry **Ezra's** name in tradition.
wrong_why: Hebrew is older; the script changed.

cards.body: Every Torah reading you hear goes back to Ezra's square: a scroll read aloud and explained. Esther's story is set among the Jews who stayed in Persia.

cards.prompt: Ezra read "from the first light until midday" to everyone who could understand. What would you want read aloud, and explained, to your whole community?

points: **539 BCE**: Cyrus lets exiles return; many stay.
**515 BCE**: the Second Temple.
Ezra reads the Torah aloud, "**translating it and giving the sense**."
Ezra adds **Shabbat afternoon** and sets **three readers, ten verses**.
Sanhedrin 21b: **Ashurit script**, the square letters.
